bib.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance

read.skipped: References skimmed only. The text mentions an Appendix (explainer comparison) that is not in the PDF.

question: Can AI explanations lead to complementary team performance (team more accurate than either human or AI alone), and do they add value over simply showing AI confidence?
hypothesis: H1 Explain-Top-1 beats Explain-Top-2; H2 Explain-Top-1 performs similar to confidence only; H3 Adaptive explanations improve performance; H4 Adaptive does better with higher-quality explanations.
contributions: Highlight that prior explanation studies all had an AI more accurate than both human and team
New experimental setup with 1626 users on three tasks evaluating explanation sources and strategies; complementary performance seen in every team condition
No significant team gain from explanations over showing confidence; explanations helped when AI was right and hurt when it erred
Adaptive Explanation (explain top-2 only when confidence is below a threshold)

method.summary: Between-subject MTurk studies on Beer and Amzbook sentiment and LSAT questions. AI accuracy was matched to human accuracy by choosing study samples. Conditions compared Human alone, Team (Conf), and teams with Explain-Top-1, Explain-Top-2 and Adaptive explanations from AI (LIME on RoBERTa) or expert sources.
method.task: AI-assisted decision making: binary sentiment classification of beer and book reviews; 4-option LSAT logical reasoning

datasets.name: Beer reviews
datasets.split: 80/20 train/test; train split oversampled to balance, further split for validation
datasets.preprocessing: target labels binarized; minority-class oversampling; 50 unambiguous test examples chosen so AI accuracy is 84% with equal FP and FN rates

datasets.name: Amzbook (Amazon book reviews)
datasets.split: 80/20 train/test; train split oversampled, validation split
datasets.preprocessing: same as Beer; AI accuracy 84% on the sample

datasets.name: ReClor (training)
datasets.source: ReClor [82], logic reasoning questions from standardized exams like LSAT and GMAT

datasets.name: LSAT study questions
datasets.preprocessing: verified not easily searchable online and not in the training data; expert explanations condensed to at most two sentences, alternatives' arguments written by hand

models.name: RoBERTa sentiment classifier (AllenNLP), one per dataset
Logistic regression (pilot only)
models.architecture: linear model, saliency from feature weights

other.note: Classifiers fine-tuned with hyper-parameter selection on validation; no values given

inference.samples: one classifier, one fixed 50-example (20 for LSAT) set per task; about 100 participants per condition (93 to 101 after filtering); all conditions same example order per dataset

parameters.explainer: LIME (post hoc saliency) on RoBERTa, shown as inline highlights
parameters.adaptive_threshold: median classifier confidence: 89.2% Beer, 88.9% Amzbook; 25 examples Explain-Top-1, 25 Explain-Top-2
parameters.adaptive composition: 18 correct and 7 incorrect examples got Explain-Top-2 in each sentiment dataset (1 incorrect, 24 correct got Explain-Top-1)
parameters.LSAT confidence scaling: top-2 class confidences scaled to sum to 100%
parameters.expert explanations: one author selected a short convincing phrase span per class

metrics.name: Decision accuracy of final human decision
metrics.definition: fraction of correct final decisions per participant, averaged, with 95% CI

metrics.name: Human-AI agreement
metrics.definition: does the final human decision match the AI suggestion

baselines: Team (Conf): AI recommendation plus confidence, no explanation
eval.protocol: Between-subject MTurk (US, approval >=97%, >=1,000 tasks). Student's T-tests with Bonferroni correction. Complementary performance = team accuracy above both human alone and AI alone. Screening: 4 of 6 reviews correct (sentiment), 2 of 2 (LSAT). Exclusions: median labeling time <2 s (3 s LSAT) or same label for all. Recruited 566 Beer, 552 Amzbook, 508 LSAT (35% passed); 84% passed for sentiment. Qualitative coding of 409 responses by two annotators, mean Cohen kappa 0.71 (sd 0.18). Subjective ratings analysed post hoc, no significance claimed. Pay: base $0.50 + $0.05 per correct (+$0.50 if >90%, +$1.00 if >95%) + $0.25 survey for sentiment; LSAT $0.30 per correct plus $1/$2/$3 at 30/50/85% accuracy.

evidence.quote: The thresholds were 89.2% for Beer and 88.9% for Amzbook.

results.claim: In Beer, the confidence-only team beat both the AI and unassisted humans (complementary performance).
results.setup: Beer, Team (Conf), ~100 participants, RoBERTa AI at 0.84 accuracy
results.quote: For Beer, providing AI recommendations and confidence to users increased their perfor- mance to (𝜇= 0.89 ± 𝜎= 0.05), surpassing both AI (0.84) and unassisted human accuracy (0.82 ± 0.09).

results.claim: Team (Conf) gained 20.1% relative over unassisted workers on LSAT.
results.setup: LSAT, Team (Conf) vs unassisted; 2.2% on Amzbook
results.quote: Team (Conf) achieved complementary performance for Amzbook and LSAT, with relative gains of 2.2% and 20.1% over unassisted workers

results.claim: Explain-Top-1 did not significantly differ from confidence only on Beer.
results.setup: Beer, Team (Explain-Top-1, AI) vs Team (Conf), ~100 per condition, T-test Bonferroni
results.quote: Team (Conf) and Team (Explain-Top-1, AI) achieved similar performance, with the accuracy being 0.89 ± 0.05 vs. 0.88 ± 0.06 respectively; the difference was insignificant (𝑧=-1.18, 𝑝=.24).
results.note: Same pattern for Amzbook (z=1.23, p=.22) and LSAT (z=0.427, p=.64).

results.claim: Explain-Top-1 vs Explain-Top-2 showed no significant difference on Beer, so H1 was not supported.
results.setup: Beer; Amzbook z=0.81 p=.42; LSAT z=0.42 p=.68
results.quote: explaining the top prediction performed marginally better than explaining the top-two predictions, but the difference was not significant (𝑧=0.85, 𝑝=.40).

results.claim: Adaptive explanations did not significantly beat confidence only on Beer or Amzbook.
results.setup: Team (Adaptive, AI) vs Team (Conf); LSAT Adaptive Expert vs Conf z=0.16 p=.87
results.quote: we did not observe any significant differences between Team (Adap- tive, AI) and Team (Conf) for Beer (𝑧=-1.02, 𝑝=.31) or Amzbook (𝑧=1.08, 𝑝=.28).

results.claim: Expert-generated adaptive explanations did not significantly beat AI-generated ones on Beer, so H4 was not supported.
results.quote: the differences in performance between Team (Adaptive, Expert) and Team (Adaptive, AI) were insignificant: Beer (𝑧=1.31, 𝑝=.19) and Amzbook (𝑧=-0.78, 𝑝=.43).

results.claim: Explanations raised accuracy when the AI was correct and lowered it when the AI erred, giving minimal net change.
results.setup: All three datasets; per-dataset evidence in Fig 4B only; Explain-Top-1 worsened accuracy when AI wrong on Beer and LSAT
results.quote: Explanations increased team performance when the system was correct, but they decreased the accuracy on examples when the system was wrong, making the net improvement minimal.

results.claim: On Amzbook, Explain-Top-1 improved accuracy by 5% over confidence only when the AI was incorrect (it decreased it on Beer and LSAT).
results.quote: when the AI was in- correct, explaining predictions on Amzbook via Explain-Top-1 improved the performance by 5% over showing confidence (Fig- ure 4B), but it decreased the performance for Beer and LSAT.

results.claim: About 70% of Beer participants rated AI assistance useful under Adaptive Expert vs 57% under Conf.
results.quote: for Beer, 70% of the participants rated AI assistance useful with Team (Adaptive, Expert) in contrast to 57% with Team (Conf).

results.claim: Collaboration approach coding: AI as Prior Guide was the most common (47%).
results.setup: Table 3 codebook; Mostly Follow AI 23 (6%), Post Check 102 (25%), Mostly Ignore 90 (22%)
results.quote: AI as Prior Guide Used AI as a starting reference point.

results.claim: Participants who mostly ignored the AI: 11% LSAT, 23% Beer, 30% Amzbook.
results.quote: only 11% of LSAT participants claimed that they mostly ignored the AI, the ratio doubled (Beer, 23%) or even tripled (Amz- book, 30%) for sentiment analysis.

results.claim: Prior studies in Table 1 found no complementary performance: AI alone beat the team in every one.
results.source: Lai et al. 2019/2020, Zhang et al., Green and Chen, Bucinca et al. and others as listed in Table 1
results.setup: Table 1 of 8 earlier studies; for example deceptive review [43] human 51.1%, AI 87.0%, team 74.6%
results.quote: complementary performance was not observed in any of these studies – in each case, adding the human to the loop decreased performance compared to if AI had acted alone.

limits: Only accuracy of decisions measured; speed and other dimensions not explored (Sec 6.1)
Crowd-workable low-stakes tasks (text classification, QA); may not generalize to high-stakes expert domains
Effect of user expertise not explored
Only two presentation styles tested: highlights and natural-language arguments
AI shown before the human decides, risking anchoring; timing not varied
Adaptive threshold simple (median confidence), a learned threshold left to future work
Subjective ratings analysed post hoc without significance tests
Explainer comparison study is referred to an Appendix not present in the PDF
Explanation sources (LIME on RoBERTa, expert highlights) date from 2020; no LLM-generated explanations tested

terms.definition: team accuracy is higher than either the human or the AI working solo
explains only the predicted class when the AI is confident, but also explains the alternative otherwise

lineage.work: Lai and Tan; Lai et al. deceptive review studies
lineage.note: Explanations help there only because AI far outperforms the team

lineage.note: AI slightly better than best team
